chapter: Fletcher as a leader and early bandmates
title: How strictly Horace led: skeleton arrangements, then full charts
summary: He gave players liberty, writing skeleton arrangements with riffs and solos and abrupt modulations, and later wrote fuller charts as readers improved.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Uh-huh. As a leader, did you -- were you pretty much a stickler for people playing very close to what was written, or was there quite a lot of freedom in the style or what they did with the notes or, you know, the types of attacks or such things as that?

Well, in those days I think I gave the individuals more liberty, especially after I found out the extent of their ability musically. I would simplify the arrangements, and I would make a lot of times what we call a skeleton arrangement, you know, and I would probably write out a riff, you know, for the first chorus. Then the solos would come in between. And a lot of times if we wanted to change

keys, and we were in a a little interlude, I'd probably take a four bar for, you know, change keys within that four bars on the piano, or either the drummer might take four bars, and we'd make an abrupt rough modulation going to the out chorus, and, of course, I always had my key men that could read real well have the lead, you know.

And it worked out real fine that way, and I found out that it made the band more relaxed because they weren't struggling, you know. So this is what I more or less leaned to in that era. But as things progressed and we got good -- I'll say better musicians reading --

-- yes -- then I began to make the arrangement full. You know, I -- instead of making it sound more like a jam deal after the first goes off, chorus and all. We actually had an interesting pattern laid out in the arrangement that we could follow because it didn't take long, number one, to rehearse this particular thing, and everybody could read. So as time marched on, this is what we did.
